blocks.x: It depends on just what time you want to talk about. I can start talking about 1910, 1908, all that. All the way back. Didn't tell nobody when you were born? All the colored bands. Really, you think jazz music wasn't originated by white people. It was originated by Negroes. And at that time it was called the Right Time Bands. More naturally, they went to North North and they called it jazz.
When were you born? I was born in 93. 93. So you remember? I remember. You remember way back.

I remember the colored bands they had all around the city of New Orleans. The Imperial Band. The Superior Band. The Olympia. The Night Millennial. The Tuxedo Band. All the colored bands. They go around. In the days when they'd give a dance, they would sing this band that would play for the dance. They'd go around on a truck. Call it a furniture wagon. Old time furniture wagon. Remember why I see people? How they moved furniture in the old days? Yeah, it was a bandwagon. Yeah. And they put sides on there, you know? With a sign. Where the dance would be. The white bands used to do the same thing. Jack Lane used to have three bands. Called Reliance Band. Number one, number two, and number three. That's why all that stuff was originated. See? From the Negroes. And you take most of the time, these colored bands, you'd get a band with eight men, seven to eight men, for a dime and a half per night. Play five hours. That was, you know, you know.
That was a dollar man had for the whole band.
A man. A man. A man. Oh yeah. That leader would get three dollars. That was big money.
I was wondering, which part of the town were you raised in? Where were you born?

I was born right here on Conti, between Dauphin and Bourbon, right where Bruce Oswald's Restore. Right there? Yes, right in the backyard I was born. Were you raised in there? I was raised all the way, I was left there in 1900. And my father went in the business on Orleans and Billory and I was around the Fifth Ward all my life. Raised in the Fifth Ward. And I was raised around a lot of colored musicians. I mean the way all the colored musicians lived in the Fifth Ward, most of them. Most of them. Every one of them. And they all just had, you know, a talent. You know what I mean? They had bands running around, taking jobs and everything. While you, many of the times we would take a job. Four men. Six dollars. Down and a half a piece. Guitar, bass, clarinet, and trumpet. And there was a big winning there, baby. From the old district. When they start putting white men in the old tenderloin district. That's the full voice for those walls. So that's why we all went there. And of course, we got a down and a half a night. We were working nine o'clock at night. We worked about four or five o'clock in the morning. As long as they're doing business, we stay there. We get paid every night. What? We were making eight, ten, twelve dollars a night, too. We're making eight, ten. So. Our salary was only a dollar and a half at night. Get all the cigarettes, all the drinks, all the eats, you know. You don't even worry about it.
Well, how old were you when you could first go in the district?

In the district, I was in short pants. To go to work at night time, I'd have to put long pants on top of my short pants. Because you wasn't allowed. Nobody, no. Yep. Well, this wasn't allowed in the district with short pants. I'd wear them, you remember the old days? We'd wear stockings. I'd put a pair of long pants over my short pants to go to work at night.
So you must have been quite young. Nothing but a kid. At least I was a fighter.
Fourteen years old, fifteen years old. And you started on the carnet?
I started on trumpet.
On trumpet. Started on trumpet. Did your folks play anything? Your father?
My father was one of the, yeah, he's a musician. He was one of the organizers of the Musicians Union. My father, that's as well. My father was one of the organizers. What was his name?
Michael. Another Michael? Yeah. Mike, yeah.

That's what we did. My son was named after him. Oh. Then my cousin was named after my daddy because my daddy christened him. And then his son was named Mike, you see? Oh, yeah. So that's why I got so damn hundred dollars in the room, you see? Oh, yeah.
And did your father play ragtime?

Well, in them days there was what you call, it wasn't ragtime in them days. My father did. You know, it was dance fans, you know, but there wasn't no pep, you know? It was a regular, legitimate resistance, you see? Of course, they played with what was called ragtime in them days, but none of them was out there the Negroes. You see, my daddy gave it up. My daddy gave up music out when I was about ten years old, you see? You know, I'll never forget I was a young kid. First time I stood out all night, played with a bunch of men old enough to be my daddy, you know? And, uh, played a dance, never forget the song as I was out of there, right on the Dominion and the Mall Street, by St. John. And I didn't come home that night next morning, we were getting home until 7 o'clock that morning. My daddy was worried. When I went home, I grabbed my corner and break it up and said, that's what you're going to do and I'll stay out all night? Because in them days and these days, it didn't 4 o'clock, 1 o'clock, it was plenty. But, you know, I was playing with a bunch of old, old fellows, you know? A bunch of old me to be my daddy, and Jesus, God, the man that we do will be. And after that night, I thought I was tops. Everybody started hiring me. All them old fellows would come get me, you see? Because I could take them. I took lessons from a man by the name of, uh, uh, Tony Maggio. And, uh, I took music lessons, reading lessons. I went to him, he was a wonderful musician. I went to him to learn how to read, you see? So, I went with my trumpet there and he seen what I could do with a trumpet. I could do more with a trumpet than he could. He said, yeah, he just, I used to amuse him. Because he could play, but he never could fake, you know? Memorize. He was, I'd amuse him. And he just take and sit down there and say, you come in and take dresses. The only thing I could do is give me music lessons. Come here without your trumpet. And I went to him and said. We were having salt, salt bed music. You know, singing. Singing salt bed music. Then I got soldier. Oh, then Jacqueline caught ahold of me. Oh, well he caught me, man. Then from there, what was Tom Brown? Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me. After Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me. Oh, after Tom Brown grabbed me, let's see, I'm trying to find, I went away. No, came down, came back again. Stood a while, went back up north, went back around Chicago. Worked with something, you know, the garage. And then most of the time, that I was in Chicago, you know, a lot of these boys down here would leave here and they'd go up nothing else and they'd get the swell there, you know what I mean? They'd want to quit, but, if you follow with them there, it wasn't like today. You know, you know, you're a man go off for you $20 or 15 hours a week more, they'd quit, gone. But we had to do that though, smart. See? And, when I went up there, I went by myself. Most of these organized bands went up there together. Then when they got up there, one fella wanted to get this fella, you know, break the band up and move naturally, and they made a fool of these. See, the only one stuck together was the Nicola Rocca. See, you heard of that. For me, when I went alone. And I didn't have no trouble with all of them. I got a job by the way. Oh. And then I got to get, Jimmy Petrello was president of the Chicago local, and his brother, Caesar. Caesar Petrello, the trombone player. So I was up in Chicago. And I was up to local. I didn't put my transfer card in. So, a fella says, you want a job for the night? I says, yeah. They had a job at Lake Geneva. I said, where in the devil is Lake Geneva? I don't know. I said, finally. He said, well, I'll pick you up. He picked me up. And I went on a job. Bunch of men sitting down there, about 10, 11 men. Never grew a horse, nothing like that. Oh. They introduced me. I sat down. Put the real voice number. I forgot those blood. Never get as wrong as I live. I was kind of shaky, you know? People were a strange man, you know what I mean? Yeah. I played the voice number, the second number. The trombone player sitting next to me was Caesar Petrello, Jimmy Petrello's brother. He put his trombone on. He says, what's your name again? I told him, he said, where you from? I said, I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man.
I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man.

I told him, he said, where you from? I said, from here. Oh, man, that's all. He says, man, wait. Meet me tomorrow at the local. Man. Yes, the next morning, the next day I meet him at the local. He introduced me. The brothers brought me. At that time, you know, I don't know if the law is the same now. You had to be in Chicago, Chicago, and then place six months before you could take a study job. Yeah, stuff right now, too. Most places, yeah. Sometimes three months. Yeah, exactly. Well, I have my transfer card. So finally, I brought me into the office, his brother, you know, and everything. So finally, he got some, I can't think, I think the brother's name is Phil Boyd, I think his name was. The only time he was called. He had a banner. He called the beach hotel. Now you know where that's at. Yeah, we're not sure. No, yeah. So I went out there, went to work out there. Stood out there about a month. And going over big. So they called me up at the local. So what they done, took me away from there, they sent me up on Broadway in Lawrence. Used to be the Green Mill one time. At that time it was called the Mont Mont Cafe. I don't know if you remember that. No. I think it's the Arabic call right now. Yeah, I know that. I went up there. Working up there. Who comes in town? Santa Piccararo. I'm home sleeping. He was working in Biloxi with Joe Polko. During the summer, the Palace Theater was closed. You remember that? Yeah. You from the Lawrence? No, I remember the Palace Theater was. So Santa comes up there. I wake, come knocking on my door. I'm sleeping about telegraph in the morning. Where you come from, boy? I just got in town. We had rehearsal that afternoon. I brought Santa. There was a book of the agent. I can't think of his name. I think it was George Edwards. So... Benson. Oh, I'm talking about the soul dog going wrong. There were a lot of Benson bands.
Benson, yeah. Benson officers. Benson, yeah.
I was a booking agent. He had a lot of them, yeah.

So I brought him up there and had to rehearse him and everything. And had a trombone player there. Santa sat in, played a couple of numbers. Man, right away this meeting wanted Santa. Took 15 trombone players. Then five though. Put him on the netted job. So we were working there. We'd go to work at 8 o'clock. To one. Five hours. To the peak north. We'd go to work at 8 o'clock. To one. Five hours. To the peak north. We'd go to about 13 men, 12, 13 men. And after one o'clock. They keep a Dixieland combination. Wow. And we skid overtime. Well, morning afters. They had another trumpet player with me. I can't remember that time. That man. Because it was such a good job. He was a wonderful musician. But he couldn't pay. In Chicago? Yes. Where would he from? Well, the morning after he'd leave. Our salary was $100 a week. But our overtime was to get $180, $170. We'd get $2 an hour overtime. $150. $160. $140. You know what I mean? As long as the people stayed through daylight.
We stayed. That's what happened. When was that? Was that after, quite a while after Tom Brown and the. Oh, Tom Brown. Yeah. He'd been up there and back.

This was around 1920. About 1920. See, Tom would've said, Tom came here to get me. And when he was up there. But I wouldn't go. You see? Because I was doing good here. You know what I mean? I made about two trips. I went to New York. In Atlantic City. I did a lot of good jobs. But you know, you take a man that's been used to. I used to get homesick. See? I was doing good. So the reason why I, when I was away, around 1925, 26, I was doing good. My home was taken sick. Me being the only son, he had a business. And I came back to see him. He was looking bad and everything. He was sinking. So I didn't go back up there. So he passed away. And I said, he told me, he says, Johnny, he says, give it up. Because you ain't gonna last that life, you know? He says, you got a business here. Take the business over and you can give it up. So I never really told me. But all of the time, he was thinking. He was thinking. He was thinking. He was thinking. He was thinking. So I didn't go back up. So he passed away. He passed away. And he told me. He says, Johnny, give it up. Because you ain't gonna last that life. You know? He says, you got a business here. Take the business over and you can give it up. So I never really told me. But all of the time, I was thinking. But all the while I wanted to go back in it, you know what I mean? I had so much, because everybody, you know, I was in demand, you see?
I could cut the stuff. Did you keep playing a little bit on weekends or any time? I don't.
What year was it you quit?

I quit in 28. See? 1928. And never played a job since. I just wanted to show you, many of the times, Santa, years back, he wanted me to say, go ahead, write this up. He said, no, of course I've got my grades and everything. I can't do it. I said, Santa, I don't want to have nothing to do with that. I'm too old for that. You know what I mean? I just. But I always got in contact with all the musicians. It was like Paul Morez, Leon Rapport, Georgia Brunis. Always, always in contact. Leon's dead. Paul's dead. You know, we heard Paul Morez. Oh, yeah. He died. All these boys. Of course. The only one now that's going kind of strong in the city here right now. It's Santa and Schalke. Schalke's not going as strong as he used to, as he was. A little while back, the last eight, nine years ago, he was going very strong. Bill plays every night. He plays, yeah. I remember because I was working for Millenberg, the Schalke's brother-in-law, Johnny Corolla. Schalke didn't even know how to hold on. He just knew how to pick up the numbers, you know, with his left hand, you know. Yeah. I said, well, I'll try to play, you know, with your right hand. Yeah, so I got in contact, keep in contact with all the boys and everything.

Well, I was wondering, speaking of names, like your father's name, what is your full name? We might be nice to have it here on the record. My full name? Johnny Lowe. And the middle name? I had it. N is my middle name, but I never used it. In case there would be any confusion, I thought it would be good to have it in the middle. Yeah, Johnny Lowe.
Well, there was several Johnny Lowe's around town.
Yeah, but there were a few playing music.
Yes. Yeah. We'd take plenty of mics. Yeah. Plenty of mics, yeah.
And they all play, I guess. Everyone.
Everyone.
Did your father fake at all?
He did, yeah. Oh, yeah, yeah. He faked? Yeah, he was fake. He was good in his days at that time. Yeah. I'm talking about many. Oh, my. Right before 1900, 1800, 1890.

Ray Lopez had told me his father was a good violin player. He was in the French Opera orchestra. Yes, in the violin player, I think. I think he played trumpet, too. I don't know. I played something. I'm not real sure. No, I was.
Tell me something. Is Jules Casdard living yet?
Yes. Yes. He travels with the races or something.

That's what I would, yeah. Yeah. Somebody's on. Jules and I all keep together. Started out Jules Casdard. Henry Brunas. Well, Henry came after. He was here. Eddie Edwards. And what's his name that died? Yellow Lunez. Remember what? Yellow Lunez.
I've got lots of his records.
Yeah. Well, what happened to him? He died. He came back. Do you know when about? Big one? About when did he die? Or do you know much about him?
Oh, he died around 20, around 1931.
Those people that aren't living were sort of interested in them, you know, because they can't speak for themselves. Yeah, yeah.

Yellow, you see his name was Al C. Nunez. We call him Yellow. Al C. Nunez. He was up north for about 15 years. And he came down here and got on the police force. More to get in the band, you know. To have him in the band, he went to the police force, you know. Yes. And he died here. And the other was a very good, wonderful faker. You see, in the days we had clarinet players. We had trombone players. But they could read. But they couldn't fake. You understand? See? They couldn't, they still, you know, other words that they called legitimate music. See? Play as is. Yeah. No improvising and nothing. But these boys had such an ear and they had rhythm. Now there's another one. I don't know if you heard of them. He was one of those. The best ball trombone player, ragtime trombone player, I think in the, that I've never heard no one play like him. Bill Gallaty. You don't want to have heard him talk about. What about? Bill Gallaty.
I've seen his picture and his son plays trombone.

His son plays trombone. Bill would take a trombone and tell you what he wouldn't do with that trombone. He'd take, when his vows wouldn't work, he'd take a hairpin and make a sprinkle. That's a son. He was a little bit of a fuck. He'd pump that thing, I'm telling you, man, just like a swat. Bill Gallaty. At that time, I'll tell you how many white bands, ragtime bands they had here. We had Christian. Frank Christian's band. You heard of him?
Yes.

Emile's brother. Emile, yeah. Frank. Bill Gallaty. Tom Brown. Jack Lane. Johnny Fisher. George Shilling was a trombone player with Johnny Fisher. Then he broke up and George Shilling went, you know, and he'd make a drum deck. And at that time, I'll tell you who was playing drum. He was a retired policeman now. Freddie Williams. Yes. Remember?
Yes, I've heard of you.
Yeah. He used to play drums with Fisher. Then he went with George Shilling. Yeah. Now that's, oh, that's 1928, 1929.
You were saying you worked with Shilling yourself.

After I came back here, I was up north, you see. Yeah. I came back here. I stood here about two years, you see. That was Spartan with Shilling. You know? Yeah. Spartan. Spartan. Shilling had the town sold out. I'll tell you how he had the town sold out with music. See, my father had a business. I was always learning how to cut meat from a child to a child. And me being the only son, my daddy always wanted me by him. You know what I mean? I wasn't no papa's boy, but still no. He was the papa and I was the boss. Everything I said, you know, he wanted me by him. So I came down there and I was with George. And I worked with my daddy in the market. So I started Spartan with George. And he had us going every night. See, at that time, I didn't need no money. I didn't need no money. I had everything I wanted. But I just loved to play music. See? So I got tired and then I wanted to take a trip again. See? Young father. You understand? But like I worked with George Shields. He had us going every night a week. I hear Bracay was with us, too. Oh, yeah. Shield, Bracay. And after I shield left, you know, I kind of got disgusted. You know what I mean? I left down a few hours. I don't know. I shield worked with us.
How many cornets did you use with Shields? Two.

We had the first one, he's dead, Harry Shannon. Then I had, we had Henrikh Konek with us. And we had Dan Tyler playing sax. We had a wonderful little jazz band. And at that time we were, we were, you see, in them days, most of these bands would run around playing with nothing but chords. You know what I mean? But they'd stick on the chords and funny facts. But George, we played music. Then we used to mix it in. You know what I mean? And we harmonized, you see? Then they had that wind jam, you know what I mean? All of them blasting music, you see? But George and I, we started playing jazz. But like, just like Paul White, we came along and made this symphonic, you know, with jazz. You understand? And that's why we were going big over there. We were going big because George would take a job. And someone would come along and they would sing, they would snap, they would sing. Well, we had the music, we played. But these other bands, you'd have, maybe about two men would lead. And the other's couldn't. But remember, you couldn't go play that stuff, you understand, son? You had, you know? But George had all good men. Everyone read but him. He's man-made of them. He said it. He always said it. He's man-made.
Who did he have in the rhythm section then?
In the rhythm section, Johnny Frisco and Eddie Hyman, who's a bass player. I know him.
Yeah? Eddie? He played with Buck Banville. Yeah, he played with Buck Banville. Buck's my uncle.

Is that right? Yeah, Buck married my, Buck's got the cornet, the cornet he's got right now, they gave, made me a present, they grow a pretty cornet in Chicago. Louis Armstrong, cost me getting that cornet. Is that right? Louis Armstrong, he brought me up to the Arab EJ manufacturers.
Oh yeah.
And they made me a present for that cornet.
Louis Armstrong. Yeah, I knew he bought one when he went on the boat.
And Buck Banville got that cornet. I seen him at the Waco about a month ago. He said, Johnny, I still got the cornet.
I haven't seen him in a long time. He was playing piano. Yeah. Out at the Plum Plants. You know where it is.

Yeah, yeah. American Legion. Robbie used to play there too, you see. Who's that? He died. Rob Aguilara. You might have heard of him. He was the secretary of the musicians union. One of those, well. Never didn't know him.
What did he do?
He played piano, played trombone, played the cornet. He died. He worked with Bobby, died. Yeah.
Well back to Happy Shilling. Lefty and, what did Frisco play? Drones. Drones.
Then Dan Taggart played saxophone.
And they did piano? No piano?
Well, no. Only when they had a place, when we had a place with a piano, I played piano.
You played piano?

Yeah. Oh, I didn't know that. When they went to the place, there were two trumpets, and they had a piano, but most of the places never had piano in the day. Oh, I know. Very few played. But, where we went, you know what I mean? So, I'm going to tell you what happened now. When saxophone's voice got popular, this is this. You know, we didn't have no saxophone players here around 1920, 1920, 1920, 1920, and there was no saxophone. There was only one saxophone player, two saxophone players in the city of New Orleans. Old man Ramos and Emil Tasso couldn't play a saxophone. Then, Dagnacca came along and played clarinet, then he bought a little, uh, supraina saxophone. You know, straight. Then, he come along with a job playing supraina saxophone and clarinet. So, finally, he bought him an E flat. Now, Schillen always used two trumpets, voice and singing. Andy was a very good trumpet player. He had always, what, breathe, pop, but he was a straight man. Me, I used to do all the, you know, play all the hot parts. And the saxophone, man, that's why. So, Dan got his saxophone. E flat. On the steamer, Sidney or Capitol, at that time was the Capitol or Sidney, I don't know what it was, the book. He came down here with a band up north. Up north, up north, up around Ohio. And they had a young fella, look just like you, about your age at that time, playing a C melody, saxophone. And it sounds so, so nice, you know what I mean? So, I said, God. So, Dan, I said, Dan, you got your supraina hole? Yeah. I said, let me have it. Come on, let me have it for about a week. Go ahead, take it. I said, well, I was done learning how to position on the dance, on the soprano. So, finally, by two weeks after that, I go, go to the malls, I buy a C melody saxophone. I said, well, I'm going to play saxophone. Mm-hm. So one night, I go to the malls, I build my corner, I build a big C melody saxophone to key. She goes, what do you got this? I start playing the C melody. But man, I want to build one trumpet. I play C melody saxophone to one to dear. Mm-hm. So finally after that I said well, of course I ruined my life. But, when I done, I left alone and went back home trouble. Just when I was getting ready to go back up north, like two months and I went back on trouble. Went over big. Made nice money. Oh we had a wonderful time. We were happy, all made money, you know what I mean? But me, I didn't need money. I got to play. But still I made the money too.
Did you have a banjo and chilling?
Sure, but trombone, banjo. He doubled up on trombone and banjo.
Oh, I see.

Oh man, we walk in the place and we got a piano man. I got another piano, chilling down the trombone. Sometimes he used banjo. Yeah. Yeah. But I'm going to tell you, talk about a sweet bass player that left it. Wonderful tone. Oh man. Yeah, we got a long time. We got a long time. I got a long time. Whatever time, I go away and I come back still. Take him a couple of months. Sure. Take me. By the way, soon he get in town, he move me to Dago. I never forget that, but he used to like me. God.
And we had a nice, a long time. Did you used to call that for any particular reason?

Yeah, more for home. More for that, you know what I mean? Yeah. We had one saxophone. We used to harmonize. Me and Kenneth, we harmonize. We never posted, we never, never prayed straight to you. You know what I mean? The melody. Yeah. Always. I take the melody, he prayed to say, you know what I mean? The harmony, you know? That's why we got by, you see. But see George, George never read. Yeah. But still he had one for him. He was a teacher in the class. He was a teacher. You know what I mean? Yeah. That's what I'm saying. You take my George and Brunner, it's the same way. I'm not going to be reading. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

You were talking about this drummer without fingers? Yeah, Pete Masarini. He played drums and he had his fingers with all little nubs. The way he used to hold them would get a kick out. Yeah, he was good huh? Yeah, Pete Masarini. He was a joke.
He could play rolls and everything? Yeah, the way he'd hold them sticks in his hands with little nubs.

I don't understand. Yeah, Pete Masarini. Joe Pelletti, Pete Masarini. Johnny Covenzano. The part of my name was Joe Holbin. He used to play guitar. Joe Holbin. Clarinet player? No, played guitar. There was no clarinet player. Yeah. The clarinet player, I'll tell you who he was. Wait, we had so many of them at that time. Wait, I'm trying to think now. The clarinet player. I think his name was Frails. These people got a seat cover place on Ramport Street. Frails. Oh, God. I'm talking about 1913, 1912. Yeah, around that time. Yeah, that's right. Pete Masarini. That's right.
Did these bands work up arrangements or did they...

We did. Did they fake it entirely? We fake it. We'd rehearse them. We'd work them up. Yeah. Did you improvise on the job at all? Very. Very. That's why everything was all improvising. Everything was all improvising. That's where jazz was originally. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

segments.chapter: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
segments.title: Jazz originated with Black New Orleans bands; Lala born 1893
segments.summary: Lala insists jazz was originated by Negroes, then called Right Time bands, and says he was born in 1893.

segments.chapter: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
segments.title: Colored bands, bandwagons and dance pay in old New Orleans
segments.summary: He recalls the Imperial, Superior, Olympia and Tuxedo bands advertising dances from furniture wagons, Jack Laine's Reliance bands, and pay of a dollar and a half a man.

segments.chapter: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
segments.title: Born on Conti Street, raised in the Fifth Ward, working the district
segments.summary: He was born on Conti, raised in the Fifth Ward among Black musicians, and describes small-band pay and nightly work in the Storyville district.

segments.chapter: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
segments.title: Playing the district as a boy in short pants, starting on trumpet
segments.summary: He went into the district at 14 or 15, wearing long pants over his short ones, and says he started on trumpet.

segments.chapter: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
segments.title: His father Michael, a musician and Musicians Union organizer
segments.summary: His father was a musician and one of the organizers of the Musicians Union; Lala's son and a cousin were named after him.

segments.title: First all-night job, lessons, Laine and Tom Brown, then Chicago and Lake Geneva
segments.summary: He recalls his father's dance music, his first all-night job, reading lessons with Tony Maggio, playing with Jack Laine and Tom Brown, and going to Chicago alone where the Petrello brothers got him work.

segments.title: Chicago jobs: Beach Hotel, Montmartre Cafe, and bringing Santo Pecora up
segments.summary: He joined the Chicago local, worked at a beach hotel and the Montmartre Cafe, and got Santo Pecora a trombone job through the Benson agency, earning good overtime.

segments.title: Dating Chicago to about 1920; homesickness and his father's illness
segments.summary: He places the Chicago period around 1920, says he was homesick and made trips to New York and Atlantic City, and came home in the mid-1920s when his father fell ill and told him to take over the family business.

segments.title: Quitting music in 1928 and keeping in touch with old bandmates
segments.summary: He quit in 1928 and never played a job again, but stayed in contact with Paul Mares, Leon Roppolo and George Brunies, and talks about Santo Pecora and Sharkey still playing.

segments.title: Lala's full name and other Johnny Lalas around town
segments.summary: The interviewers ask for his full name for the record and note that several Johnny Lalas played music in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Musicians and ragtime bands of the time
segments.title: His father as a faker before 1900; Ray Lopez's father
segments.summary: Lala says his father could fake well in the 1890s; the interviewer mentions Ray Lopez's father playing violin in the French Opera orchestra.

segments.chapter: Musicians and ragtime bands of the time
segments.title: Jules Cassard and the late Yellow Nunez
segments.summary: He asks after Jules Cassard, names old colleagues, and says Yellow Nunez died around 1931.

segments.chapter: Musicians and ragtime bands of the time
segments.title: Al Nunez, fakers versus readers, and trombonist Bill Gallaty
segments.summary: He describes Al C. Nunez joining the police band, contrasts natural fakers with legitimate readers, and praises Bill Gallaty as the best ragtime trombone player he ever heard, with tricks like fixing his slide with a hairpin.

segments.chapter: Musicians and ragtime bands of the time
segments.title: White ragtime bands of the era and George Schilling's drummer
segments.summary: He lists the white ragtime bands (Christian, Gallaty, Tom Brown, Jack Laine, Johnny Fisher), and says Schilling came out of Fisher's band with drummer Freddie Williams.

segments.title: Working with George Schilling's band after returning from the north
segments.summary: Back in New Orleans he worked nightly with Schilling, whose band played arranged jazz with a good lineup and a rhythm section of Johnny Frisco and Eddie Hyman.

segments.title: Buck Banville and the cornet Louis Armstrong helped him get
segments.summary: Eddie Hyman played with Buck Banville; Lala says Armstrong took him to the manufacturers who gave him a cornet, which Banville now has.

segments.title: Rob Aguilara, union secretary and multi-instrumentalist
segments.summary: He briefly describes Rob Aguilara, secretary of the musicians union, who played piano, trombone and cornet and has died.

segments.title: Schilling's instrumentation and Lala taking up saxophone in New Orleans
segments.summary: He gives the band's lineup, says he played piano where there was one, and tells how saxophones first arrived around 1920 and how he bought a C melody sax.

segments.title: Banjo and trombone doubling and harmonizing in the band
segments.summary: He discusses the band member who doubled trombone and banjo and how he and a saxophonist harmonized, with Lala on melody.

segments.title: Pete Masarini, the drummer with no fingers, and his band
segments.summary: He recalls drummer Pete Masarini, who played with finger stumps, and others in that band including Joe Pelletti, Joe Holbin and a clarinetist around 1912-13.

segments.title: Whether the bands worked up arrangements or improvised
segments.summary: He says they rehearsed and worked up numbers but everything was improvised, which is where jazz began.
